newsitem.title: CANADA: Soft landing for Canadian dollar, economists say.
newsitem.headline: Soft landing for Canadian dollar, economists say.

text.p: Canada's shaky dollar has bottomed out and will likely weather the storm of an impending U.S. interest rate hike, economists said on Monday.
"My feeling is that the worst is over," said Reid Farrill, corporate foreign exchange adviser for CIBC Wood Gundy. "The market has factored this in and the Canada dollar should begin to firm up."
"The markets have already bought (U.S.) dollars in anticipation of a rate hike," Farrill added.
The Canadian dollar, which was forecast to outperform other G7 currencies in 1997, has lost more than two percent of its value against a surging U.S. dollar in the past month.
Last week, Canada's dollar reached a one-year low when it broke past C$1.3800 (US$0.7299). The currency only stabilized after the Bank of Canada intervened to buy Canada dollars.
Most economists saw only a slight hit for the dollar if the Bank of Canada did not match an expected 25 basis point hike by the U.S. Federal Reserve on Tuesday.
The dollar should not weaken past last week's C$1.3825 (US$0.7233), one trader said. In late trading on Monday, the Canadian dollar was at C$1.3791 (US$0.7251).

Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen said last week that the central bank did not necessarily have to match any Fed rate hike, although adding his comments should not be interpreted as a pledge not to raise Canadian rates.

"If the bank holds tight, even though the Fed hikes, the Canadian dollar will probably fare much better than it did in 1994-95 after the Mexican peso crisis," said Mark Levesque, economist with Bank of Nova Scotia.
Economists said that Canada's solid economic fundamentals would also help buttress any sudden fall in the currency, economists said.
Canada's GDP was expected to grow by 3.3 percent this year, while inflation would likely remain in the central bank's target range of one to three percent.
Statistics Canada, the federal government's statistical agency, reported last Thursday that retail sales rose a better than expected 1.4 percent in January.
But not everyone was sold on the idea of a soft landing for the Canadian dollar in the event of a Fed hike.
The Bank of Canada could not afford to be complacent amid rising U.S. interest rates, said Michael Gregory, economist and strategist with Lehman Brothers.
"If they (the central bank) don't go immediately, I think the Canadian dollar will take it on the nose," Gregory said.
